_: Shoe-sole rubber: a vulcanised, carbon-black (or silica) filled SBR / natural rubber (NR) compound, Shore A ~65 (55-70), black, moulded tread, at ~20 C. Hyperelastic (Mooney-Rivlin / Ogden) and viscoelastic: its grip comes from adhesion on dry smooth floors and from hysteresis (the rubber draping over asperities and losing energy) on wet or rough ones, both shifting with speed and temperature (WLF). Partners research lane 11-07 (PARTNERS.md).

alpha.src: matte moulded rubber (mould texture Ra ~2-10 um); wear polishes the contact patch slightly; a water film makes it glossy

n.src: E: recalled from the Polymer Handbook (POLYHB), not re-read: natural rubber nD 1.519, SBR ~1.53

albedo.src: carbon black at 20-50 phr absorbs nearly everything (black soles); gum-rubber (crepe, tan) and silica soles are lighter

static.src: E: ETB re-read 11-08 gives only sliding values for rubber on concrete (dry 0.6-0.85, wet 0.45-0.75), no static; Wikipedia's friction table (secondary, re-read 11-08) gives concrete-rubber static 1.0 dry, 0.30 wet; the bands dry [0.8, 1.0] and wet [0.5, 0.7] kept as E (the wet band sits above Wikipedia's 0.30); oily E (ENISO20345 glycerine-on-steel pass thresholds 0.13-0.18, recalled, show how low it goes)

kinetic.src: ETB friction table re-read 11-08: rubber on dry concrete 0.6-0.85, wet concrete 0.45-0.75 (sliding); dry 0.8 and wet 0.5 sit inside (the src had said kinetic dry 0.8, wet 0.5); oily E

friction.counterface: concrete / ceramic tile (ETB); per-floor values in pairs/solids.json (stone), pairs/world.json (soil, sand, gravel, ice) and pairs/partners.json (steel, aluminium, wood, glass)

mechanism.v: mu = mu_adhesion (dry, smooth: real contact area x interfacial shear; very high on clean glass) + mu_hysteresis (rough: viscoelastic loss as the rubber drapes over asperities, needs tan_delta at the asperity frequency v/lambda). Water or oil kills the adhesion term; on a smooth wet floor nothing is left (slip); on a rough wet floor hysteresis keeps grip. Friction peaks near ~1 cm/s-1 m/s and rises as temperature falls toward Tg (until glassy).
mechanism.src: PERSSON01 / TANAKA16: wet friction ~ hysteresis, dry adds adhesion; PERSSON25 dry adhesion dominates, lubricated = bulk viscoelastic loss

surface_energy_mJ_m2.src: E: recalled from the Polymer Handbook (POLYHB), Wu 1982 (WU82), not re-read: POLYHB / WU82 natural rubber ~34-36, SBR ~31-33 mJ/m2, nearly all dispersive

tack.v: vulcanised sole: little tack (not sticky) but a large real contact area on smooth clean surfaces: rubber on clean glass can exceed mu 1-2 (adhesive)

restitution.src: e = sqrt(rebound resilience): resilience 0.45 (sole compounds 0.40-0.55; JIS K 6255 floor 40 % in PAT11118037); the rest is hysteresis

collision_thickness_mm.src: numerical offset: the sole deforms itself (its own FE / XPBD volume), so the offset only has to stop pass-through at tread-lug scale (lugs 2-5 mm); 0.2 mm is below the lug relief

E_MPa.src: GENT58 relation re-read 11-08 via Wikipedia 'Shore durometer' (Gent 1958, Rubber Chem Technol 31:896-906): E = 0.0981 (56 + 7.62336 S)/(0.137505 (254 - 2.54 S)) MPa, S = Shore A 65 gives 4.43; the 60A Mooney-Rivlin pair below gives 6(C10+C01) = 3.55 MPa, consistent

contact_stiffness_kPa_per_mm.src: E / sole thickness (10 mm outsole): the unconfined layer stiffness; a laterally confined thin pad is stiffer (shape factor), and lugs softer

contact_damping_ratio.src: zeta = -ln e / sqrt(pi^2 + ln^2 e) from e 0.67

response_time_ms.src: Hertz t = 2.87 (m^2/(R E*^2 v))^0.2, 1 kg rigid sphere R 25 mm at 1 m/s on a thick block, E* = E/(1 - 0.25): the sole's own pulse is ~10 ms; a heel strike is longer (~50-100 ms) because the body and the heel pad set it

wave_speed_m_s.src: sqrt(G/rho), G = E/3 (incompressible); sqrt((K + 4G/3)/rho), K ~2 GPa, rho 1150: rubber shears slowly (lugs visibly squirm) but resists volume change

damping_ratio.src: from restitution; the material loss factor is deform.viscoelastic.tan_delta

solver._: Incompressible: when squashed it bulges sideways (volume kept, nu 0.4995); a solver must not let it lose volume. Tread lugs shear and squirm on contact.

water_contact_angle_deg.src: E: recalled from the Polymer Handbook (POLYHB), not re-read: POLYHB natural / SBR rubber advancing ~95-100 deg (hydrophobic; fillers, waxes and mould release shift it)

oil_contact_angle_deg.src: oils spread on (and slowly swell) NR / SBR: diene rubbers are not oil-resistant (nitrile soles are)

porosity.src: solid moulded rubber vs blown (crepe-like, microcellular) soles

water_absorption.src: vulcanised filled SBR / NR: under ~1 % by mass after long immersion

oil_absorption.v: NR / SBR swell in mineral oil and fuels (tens of % volume over days); grease on the floor both lubricates and slowly softens the sole
oil_absorption.src: rubber chemistry practice (ASTM D471 swell tests)

v.position: negative: a rubber sole walking on carpet / wool (0), nylon (+30) takes electrons, the body is left +; on PP / PVC floors (-90 / -100) it can charge the other way

resistivity_ohm_m.src: E: recalled from EN ISO 20345 (ENISO20345), not re-read: carbon black at sole loadings rarely percolates: ordinary soles are insulating (> 1e9 ohm through the sole per ENISO20345 class I insulating), ESD footwear 1e5-1e8 ohm, conductive < 1e5

permittivity_rel.src: NR 2.4-2.7 unfilled; carbon-black filled compounds higher

v.dry_RH<30: minutes (body voltage builds to kV on carpet)

charge_decay_s.src: follows sole resistance and humidity; why winter carpet shocks happen

hardness.src: KURARAY13 shoe-sole compounds Shore A 55-65; work and hiking soles 65-75

abrasion.src: PAT11118037 sole compound DIN abrasion <= 150 mm3; ordinary soles 100-250 mm3 E; carbon black resists wear better than silica / gum

density_kg_m3.src: filled SBR / NR sole compounds 1.10-1.25 g/cm3 (gum NR 0.93, carbon black 1.8 at 30-60 phr)

E_MPa.src: GENT58 (relation re-read 11-08 via Wikipedia 'Shore durometer') from Shore A 65 (small-strain): 4.43 MPa

poisson.src: rubber is nearly incompressible, nu 0.499-0.4999 (bulk ~1000x shear)

bulk_MPa.src: E: recalled from textbook / trade ranges, not re-read: NR / SBR bulk modulus ~1.9-2.1 GPa (rubber handbooks)

C10_MPa.src: CALCULIX60A C10 0.474 at 60A scaled by E(65A)/E(60A) = 1.25

C10_MPa_60A.src: CALCULIX60A generic 60 Shore A fit from a 2018 paper, not experimentally verified (the poster's caveat): taken as a starting point

ogden_NR_gum_reference.src: E: recalled from Ogden 1972 (OGDEN72), not re-read: OGDEN72 three-term fit to Treloar's unfilled vulcanised NR (uniaxial, equibiaxial, pure shear): the shape of the large-strain stiffening; a filled sole is ~3-4x stiffer at small strain

tan_delta.src: TPV19 tan delta at 0 C 0.35 'an ordinary vulcanised rubber sole'; 23 C and -30 C E (SBR loss peak at Tg)

Tg_C.src: E: recalled from textbook / trade ranges, not re-read: rubber handbooks: high-Tg SBR is chosen for wet grip

rebound_resilience.src: PAT11118037 floor 40 % (JIS K 6255); NR gum ~0.7, filled sole 0.4-0.55

relaxation_s.src: filled rubber relaxes over a broad spectrum (power law); a WLF shift ties rate and temperature: 10x speed ~ -7 to -10 C

mullins_payne.v: first stretch softens a filled rubber (Mullins, 10-30 % on reload); stiffness falls with strain amplitude above ~1 % (Payne): a new sole flexes stiffer than a worn-in one
mullins_payne.src: E: recalled from rubber physics (Mullins 1969; Payne 1962), not re-read: the shape of the softening only

strength_tensile_MPa.src: KURARAY13 soft sole compounds tensile 10-15 MPa

tear_kN_m.src: filled SBR / NR tear strength (ASTM D624) typical

sim._: Volume-preserving hyperelastic (Mooney-Rivlin from the block above) with a Prony / fractional damping; XPBD volume constraint stiff, deviatoric compliant.

conductivity_W_mK.src: E: recalled from textbook / trade ranges, not re-read: filled NR / SBR 0.2-0.3 W/mK (gum NR 0.13-0.15; carbon black raises it)

heat_capacity_J_kgK.src: E: recalled from textbook / trade ranges, not re-read: NR ~1880-1900 J/kgK

effusivity.src: sqrt(k rho c) = sqrt(0.25 x 1150 x 1900) W s^0.5 m^-2 K^-1

contact_temp_with_skin_C.src: SKINTH: T = (e_skin 33 + e 20)/(e_skin + e), skin 33 C on material 20 C, e_skin 1188; lower = feels colder

emissivity.src: EMIS_ETB re-read 11-08: rubber hard glossy plate 0.94, natural hard 0.91, natural soft 0.86, foam 0.90; 0.93 kept for a hard filled sole (the cited band 0.92-0.94 was not the table's)

wet.src: water film: glossy, adhesion gone; on smooth floors friction collapses (pairs/solids.json polished stone wet 0.09-0.3), on rough it holds through hysteresis; tread channels drain the film

oily.src: oil / grease: worse than water (higher viscosity film); NR / SBR also swell

cold.src: at about -10 to 0 C an SBR sole stiffens (~2x) and its loss rises toward Tg: grip on cold dry rough ground rises, on ice it falls (pairs/world.json ice near 0 C 0.03-0.1)

frozen_glassy.src: below Tg (~-50 C SBR, -70 C NR) it turns leathery-glassy (E ~1 GPa): it no longer drapes over asperities, slides like hard plastic

new_mould_release.src: new soles carry mould-release and bloom (waxes, antiozonants): slippery until scuffed off

worn.src: worn smooth: less tread to drain water, so wet grip falls on smooth floors

ETB.cite: The Engineering ToolBox, Friction and friction coefficients for some common materials
ETB.lic: free web reference; numbers used as facts (friction table re-read 11-08)

ALPHALAB.cite: Lee B / AlphaLab Inc. (TriField) triboelectric table, charge affinity nC/J (positive = charges +); zero = the average conductor (all metals about equal); read via the storiesinfabric.blogspot.com reprint 11-07
ALPHALAB.lic: free web table, reproduction only in whole: single numbers used as facts, table not copied STUDY ONLY (P13)

SKINTH.cite: skin thermal inputs for contact temperature: k 0.37 W/mK, c 3500 J/kgK (Duck 1990 tissue tables, typical), rho 1090 from skin.body

GENT58.cite: Gent AN. On the relation between indentation hardness and Young's modulus. Trans Inst Rubber Ind 34:46-57 (1958); reprinted Rubber Chem Technol 31(4):896-906 (1958), doi:10.5254/1.3542351: E(MPa) = 0.0981(56 + 7.62336 S)/(0.137505(254 - 2.54 S))
GENT58.lic: paywalled; the relation re-read 11-08 as quoted in Wikipedia 'Shore durometer' (CC BY-SA text; a formula is a fact)

CALCULIX60A.cite: CalculiX discourse 'Approximation rubber shore 60' and R. Smith, Mooney-Rivlin rubber data for CalculiX: 60 Shore A C10 0.474 MPa, C01 0.118 MPa (from a 2018 paper, not experimentally verified; 'use at your own risk')
CALCULIX60A.lic: public forum / personal web page; numbers used as estimates

OGDEN72.cite: Ogden RW. Large deformation isotropic elasticity: on the correlation of theory and experiment for incompressible rubberlike solids. Proc R Soc Lond A 326:565-584 (1972), fit to Treloar (1944) NR data
OGDEN72.lic: paywalled; fitted constants used as facts (recalled from the source, not re-read 11-07)

KURARAY13.cite: Kuraray Elastomer, RRF13 rubber compounds for shoe soles with SEPTON BIO series: sole hardness Shore A 55-65, tensile 10-15 MPa
KURARAY13.lic: manufacturer technical note; numbers used as facts

PAT11118037.cite: US Patent 11,118,037, Rubber composition for shoe sole and molded article: SBR / SBS sole, DIN 53516 abrasion <= 150 mm3; rebound resilience floor 40 % (JIS K 6255) in the related claims
PAT11118037.lic: US patent, public domain; numbers used as facts

TPV19.cite: Thermoplastic vulcanizate (SSBR) shoe-sole study: tan delta at 0 C of 0.35 'represents an ordinary vulcanized rubber sole material in the market' (as found by web search 11-07; paper not opened)
TPV19.lic: journal article; number used as a fact (source not opened)

PERSSON01.cite: Persson BNJ. Theory of rubber friction and contact mechanics. J Chem Phys 115:3840 (2001); with the Springer chapter on wet/dry rubber friction (hysteresis wet, adhesion added dry)

PERSSON25.cite: Persson group, steel sliders on rubber, dry vs silicone-oil lubricated (arXiv 2505.16943, 2025): dry adhesion dominant, lubricated = bulk viscoelastic dissipation

TANAKA16.cite: Tanaka et al. Mechanical Engineering Journal 3(1) 15-00084 (2016): filled rubber on rough surfaces, hysteresis friction via Persson theory carries most of the friction, adhesion raises it

ENISO20345.cite: EN ISO 20345:2021 / ISO 13287 safety footwear slip resistance: SRB on steel with glycerine, flat >= 0.18, heel forward >= 0.13; SRA ceramic + SLS solution, flat >= 0.32, heel >= 0.28; electrical classes (antistatic 1e5-1e9 ohm)
ENISO20345.lic: paywalled standard; thresholds used as facts (recalled from the source, not re-read 11-07)

POLYHB.cite: Brandrup J, Immergut EH, Grulke EA (eds). Polymer Handbook, 4th ed. (Wiley 1999) / Mark JE (ed). Physical Properties of Polymers Handbook: refractive index, surface energy, thermal values of NR, SBR, PA66, CA, ABS, PP
POLYHB.lic: paywalled handbooks; single numbers used as facts (recalled from the source, not re-read 11-07)

WU82.cite: Wu S. Polymer Interface and Adhesion. Marcel Dekker (1982): polymer surface energies (dispersive / polar)
WU82.lic: book; numbers used as facts (recalled from the source, not re-read 11-07)
